##### Motivation: how do we use the model for extrapolation? {#sec-pri-599b}

[**Graphical representation of extrapolation**]{#sec-pri-599b-graphical}

Extrapolation is performed similarly to [interpolation](#sec-pri-599a). For example, the predicted value at temperature $T$ = 375 and time $t$ = 28 is indicated by the "X":

![Extrapolation point marked outside the design](advanced-topics/images/design-square-extrap-point.svg){#fig-pri-599b-extrap-point width=65%}

and is computed by substituting the values $X_1$ = +2.0 ($T$=375) and $X_2$ = +0.8 ($t$=28) into the prediction equation

$$\hat{Y} = 5 + 2 X_{2} + X_{1}$$

yielding a predicted value of 8.6.

::: {.callout-note}
Independently recomputing $X_2$ using the same coding formula established on the [interpolation page](#sec-pri-599a-predicting) ($X_2 = (t - 25) / 5$, since $t = 25$ is the design center and 5 minutes corresponds to one coded unit) gives $X_2 = (28-25)/5 = 0.6$, not the $X_2 = 0.8$ stated above -- and substituting $X_2 = 0.6$ yields $\hat{Y} = 8.2$, not 8.6. NIST's own stated $X_2 = 0.8$ is the value actually needed to reach their stated $\hat{Y} = 8.6$, but it is internally inconsistent with $t = 28$ under their own coding scheme ($X_2 = 0.8$ corresponds to $t = 29$). We report both NIST's stated values and our independently recomputed ones below rather than silently reconciling them.
:::

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
x1 <- (375 - 325) / 25
x2_formula <- (28 - 25) / 5
x2_nist <- 0.8
tibble::tibble(
  source = c("Recomputed from t = 28", "NIST stated"),
  x1 = x1,
  x2 = c(x2_formula, x2_nist),
  y_hat = 5 + 2 * x2 + x1
)

```

Thus:

![Predicted value for the extrapolated point](advanced-topics/images/design-square-extrap-value.svg){#fig-pri-599b-extrap-value width=65%}

[**Pseudo-data**]{#sec-pri-599b-pseudo-data}

The predicted value from the modeling effort may be viewed as pseudo-data, data obtained without the experimental effort. Such "free" data can add tremendously to the insight via the application of graphical techniques (in particular, the [contour plots](#sec-pri-59a)) and can add significant insight and understanding as to the nature of the response surface relating $Y$ to the $X$'s.

But, again, a final word of caution: the "pseudo data" that results from the modeling process is exactly that, pseudo-data. It is **not** real data, and so the model and the model's predicted values must be validated by additional confirmatory (real) data points. A more balanced approach is that:

> Models may be trusted as "real" [that is, to generate predicted values and contour curves], but must always be verified [that is, by the addition of confirmatory data points].

The rule of thumb is thus to take advantage of the available and recommended model-building mechanics for these 2-level designs, but do treat the resulting derived model with an equal dose of both optimism and caution.

[**Summary**]{#sec-pri-599b-summary}

In summary, the motivation for model building is that it gives us insight into the nature of the response surface along with the ability to do interpolation and extrapolation; further, the motivation for the use of the cumulative residual standard deviation plot is that it serves as an easy-to-interpret tool for determining a good and parsimonious model.
